title: The Skye Boat Song
description: Harold Boulton's Jacobite boat song from Songs of the North, for 2 to 4 singers: the chorus, the first two verses (the storm, and Flora's watch over the sleeping prince) and the chorus again. The soprano sings the tune, an air taken down from Hebridean boatmen and finished by Anne Campbell Macleod, over Malcolm Lawson's harmony from the book, set for voices. Lively and well accented, as the book asks.

licence.words: public domain: Harold Boulton (1859 to 1935); printed by 1888 (D. H. Edwards, Modern Scottish Poets, eleventh series, Brechin, preface dated November 1888) and with its tune in 1888 (Laura Alexandrine Smith, The Music of the Waters, pp. 90 to 91), both with "Thunder-clouds"; "Thunder-claps", as sung here and today, in Songs of the North (Cramer, an undated reprint) and, dated, in Our National Songs (Cramer, copyright 1923)
licence.tune: public domain: a traditional Hebridean boat air (four bars) completed by Anne Campbell Macleod (four bars), printed by 1888; Anne Campbell Macleod, later Lady Wilson, died 1921 (Who's Who 1923, p. 2966, under Wilson, Sir James: 'm. 1888, Anne Campbell (d. 1921), d. of late Very Rev. Norman Macleod'; named as Songs of the North's 'A. C. Macleod [Lady Anne Campbell Wilson]' in the Boston Public Library's Allen A. Brown catalogue, p. 224)
licence.arrangement: Malcolm Lawson's harmony (public domain: Lawson died 1918, by the National Portrait Gallery's catalogue, 1981), from his piano accompaniment in Songs of the North: his chords kept bar by bar (G, D7, G and C, G in the chorus; E minor, A minor, E minor and B augmented, E minor, G, A minor, E minor over B and B augmented, E minor in the verse), his drone bass in the chorus turned into a sung bass line (D7 over C at "wing" and "king", G over B at "on-ward" and "o-ver"), his verse bass kept (E, A, B, E; then G, A, B, E), with D-sharp under his B augmented chord so the trio has its third, the alto and tenor written by Stackapella so the duet and trio keep the third (the duet sings the B augmented as G over B), the alto, tenor and bass holding "boat" through the tune's "like a", with breaths written in for beginners
licence.source: melody, words and harmony from Songs of the North, gathered together from the Highlands and Lowlands of Scotland, vol. I, edited by A. C. Macleod and Harold Boulton, the music arranged by Malcolm Lawson (J. B. Cramer and Co., London, undated, catalogued 19--; first published by Field and Tuer, the Leadenhall Press, London), no. V, "Skye Boat Song (Jacobite)", pp. 18 to 20, "Four bars taken down from Hebridean boatmen, four bars added by A. C. Macleod", in G in 6/8 (a dotted crotchet is one beat here) and written here in G; read from the scans at archive.org/details/31761034118778/page/n37 (p. 18), page/n38 (p. 19) and page/n39 (the words, p. 20); the tune checked against J. S. Blackie, Scottish Song (William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London, 1889), pp. 239 to 240, archive.org/details/scottishsongitsw00blacrich/page/n254 (the same tune in G, its "the" in "bird on the wing" printed G, not A as Songs of the North prints it there and at "be king"), and Our National Songs, ed. Harold Boulton, no. 10, pp. 32 to 36 (J. B. Cramer, London, 1923, arranged by Arthur Somervell, not used for the harmony), archive.org/details/31761034962274/page/n39 (the same tune, "Thunderclaps"); sung as the book directs ("Chorus to begin, and after each verse"): chorus, verse 1, chorus, verse 2, chorus, verses 3 and 4 (Culloden, the burned homes) left out; breaths written in for beginners: "cry;" and "Skye." (beats 6, 14, 38, 46 and 70) and "air;", "dare.", "bed.", "head." (22, 30, 54, 62) held a dotted crotchet, not a dotted minim, and a dotted crotchet's rest before the next line; the last "Skye." kept as a dotted minim, without the tied crotchet and pause printed for the last time, so the song ends on a bar line; Harold Boulton 1859 to 1935, Malcolm Lawson died 1918
